sources.note: Contributed the AI-tell catalog. Filtered from 37 patterns to the ~21 that fire in a technical register and compressed to one-line rows.
Contributed the composition rules. Strunk's 18 rules condensed to the 8 that apply to short technical prose. The elements-of-style reference files were dropped.

modifications: Authoring-first rather than editing-first, and narrowed to the prose that lives in a repository or on a forge. Dropped humanizer's draft, audit, and final rewrite loop, its travel-blog example, and its DETECTION GUIDANCE and PERSONALITY AND SOUL sections. Voiced and long-form prose stays with humanizer. Dropped the curly-quote pattern, since a model emits straight ASCII, and the Wikipedia-article framing of the significance, notability, and challenges patterns.

Added what no upstream carries: a content rule that git prose says why rather than what, a default of silence for the commit body, worked examples shaped like real commits, and a check list that runs before a draft is returned. That list names the anti-patterns of agent-written prose, among them the tool-attribution trailer, the recap section, and the caveat that changes nothing.
Inverted upstream's diff-anchored-writing rule for commits, changelogs, and migration guides, where narrating the change is the job.
Condensed DO NOT TOUCH to five lines and extended it to identifiers, CLI flags, and file paths.
Renamed from repo-prose to oss-writing on migration into oss-kit.

Split the body so that everything conditional loads only where it is needed, per R-SKL-07. The tell catalog moved to references/tells.md, which loads when a draft reads padded, generic, or promotional. Added a nominalized gerund chain row to that catalog, folded prefer-the-common-word into the AI-vocabulary row, and folded synonym drift into elegant variation, because both already existed there under other names. Attached a reason to every hard constraint, and moved the worked examples into <example> tags, following Anthropic's context engineering post and its prompting guidance.

Added composition rules paraphrased from ASD-STE100 Issue 9, and its sentence, paragraph, and noun-stack figures as limits: 20 words in an instruction, 25 in any other sentence, six sentences in a paragraph, three nouns in a stack. They were stated as signals to split rather than limits, until a later change measured that a signal does not bind. What survives of the rules themselves is one instruction per sentence, the noun-stack cap, and writing for translation with no idioms. ASD-STE100 is copyright ASD and an EU registered trademark. No rule text, dictionary entry, or other wording was copied from it. The rules were written from its principles and it is cited by name. Its approved-word dictionary and no-gerund rule were rejected as a poor fit for software prose. Public secondary material on it was read on 2026-07-28 to confirm the figures this skill had carried on trust. The specification itself is paywalled and was not read.

Made the commit and change-request body default to none. The per-artifact content table it replaced listed what a body carries, which read as a checklist to cover. A template's required sections still win, since they decide whether a section appears where this decides how much it gets. Replaced the bad-and-good example pairs for git prose with finished artifacts, each named for what earned its body. The bad halves were demonstrating the padded output the skill was still producing. Pairs stay in references/tells.md, where the contrast is the lesson.

Added a hard constraint against a clause that tells the reader how to weigh a fact just stated. Upstream's closer patterns are all promotional. The defensive form is not upbeat, carries none of the significance-inflation vocabulary, and passes the sentence-length caps, so nothing already in the skill fired on it.

Rebuilt the body from the cited sources, which were re-read on 2026-07-28, rather than trimmed. Each source was distilled and then filtered against Anthropic's skill-authoring criterion, that a skill adds only context the model does not already have. Most of what the sources say fails that filter and was cut: imperative mood, the 50-character subject, small focused change requests, second person, active voice as a bare instruction, and Conventional Commits in full, which is a 2019 standard a repository declares for itself. Four things this fork had added went with them: the RFC 2119 keyword section, the per-artifact content table covering issues and ADRs, the body-trigger ladder, and the ban on narrating the author's route to a fix. What survived is what changes the output. From Git's SubmittingPatches: the three-part body order, the status quo in the present tense, self-containment over a link, splitting a change whose description runs long, and git show -s --pretty=reference for citing a prior commit. From GitHub's review guidance: the shape of a review comment. From the Google developer documentation style guide, used under CC BY 4.0: the timeless-language word list, the ban on inflecting a code element, and putting a condition before its instruction. The body is 101 lines where it was 208, and what left it split by artifact into references for commits and change requests, for code review, and for documentation. references/forge-rendering.md is deleted, which is a capability loss rather than a relocation: nothing here documents per-forge rendering any more. The one clause that changes what gets typed stays in the body, which is to keep the subject to 72 characters, counting any number the forge appends on squash.

Ported three things from an independently researched skill draft that was evaluated against this one: the rule-to-checker map in references/linting.md, a flattened banned-word list for a substitution linter, and Conventional Comments labels as an option for a repository that has adopted them. All three land in references rather than in the body that loads every time. A four-arm blind evaluation decided that placement, twenty-four judgements over two rounds with the outputs shuffled and the judges shown no skill. A fused variant that merged both rule sets into its core scored 100 percent on every mechanical check and placed last on judged quality, never once first, because stacked sentence caps and one-instruction-per-sentence fragment the prose. This skill scored 28 Borda in both rounds, before and after the port, so the additions cost nothing in judged quality.

Sharpened the consequence condition after a 100-prompt evaluation found this skill placing last on trivial-looking commits. It suppressed a body whenever the diff looked small, regardless of whether the facts earned one. Two clauses fix it: the condition reaches a change whose safety rests on a fact the diff cannot show, and the size of the change does not decide. Measured unlabelled on 59 tasks, the skill moved from 0 of 7 earned bodies to 7 of 7, while still writing none of the 27 unearned. An unaided model scores 56 of 59 on the same set, writing two bodies that are not earned. The check list also regained a first step that counts the longest sentence, the only rule here that needs counting rather than recognizing. That step took the worst prompt from four over-length sentences to one, and the Opus arm from 98 to 99 percent.

Narrowed the scope twice, against upstream and against this fork's own earlier position, and settled one term. Guidance for error messages, log lines, and code comments is gone, because those strings live inside source files and this kit does not edit code. A change-request description no longer has to account for every changed file. That rule had come from a judge panel rather than a source. The reviewer already has the file list, and restating it is the noise this skill bans. The artifact is a change request throughout rather than a pull request, since forge scope is GitHub and GitLab. The frontmatter keeps PR, which is what a user types when asking for one.

Gave a change-request description a shape of its own, which no upstream carries. It had been governed by the rules written for a commit body, inherited by sitting in the same reference: default to silence, no markup, one paragraph per line. A description is rendered on the forge and read before the diff, so it now uses the markup the forge renders, gives a change with separable parts one bullet each, and earns its length from what review needs. This is narrower than the per-forge rendering reference deleted in 0.5.1, which stays deleted. What returns is the clause that changes what gets typed, not the column widths and newline handling of either forge.
